lessons.title: The AWS Root Account and Why You Stop Using It

slots.practicalActivity: Sign in to your own AWS account's root user once to confirm MFA is not yet enabled, go to IAM > Security credentials and turn on MFA using an authenticator app, then create a real IAM user (e.g. admin-yourname) with the AdministratorAccess managed policy attached, sign out, and sign back in as that IAM user instead of root for the rest of this course.
slots.deliverable: Confirmation that root now has MFA enabled, a working IAM administrator user you successfully signed in as, and a written list of the short set of tasks that still genuinely require root.

lessons.title: IAM Users, Groups, and Policies

slots.practicalActivity: In IAM, create a group named Reporting-Readonly, create a new IAM user with no initial permissions, add that user to the group, and attach a custom least-privilege policy you write yourself (modeled on the lesson's Allow/s3:GetObject example) scoped to exactly one real S3 bucket name in your account. Sign in as that user and confirm reading a different bucket is denied.
slots.deliverable: A real IAM group with a custom JSON least-privilege policy attached, one user placed in it, and a captured Access Denied result proving the user can read only the one bucket the policy names.

lessons.title: IAM Roles and Why They Beat Long-Lived Keys

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real IAM role with a trust policy allowing the EC2 service to assume it, attach a policy granting s3:GetObject on one bucket, attach the role to a running EC2 instance as an instance profile, and from inside the instance run aws s3 cp to pull a file from that bucket with zero access keys configured anywhere on the instance. Run aws sts get-caller-identity from inside the instance to see the assumed-role identity.
slots.deliverable: A real EC2 instance successfully reading from S3 via an attached IAM role/instance profile, with get-caller-identity output showing the assumed-role identity and no access keys ever configured on the instance.

lessons.title: AWS Organizations and Account Hierarchy Basics

slots.practicalActivity: In AWS Organizations, create at least one Organizational Unit (e.g. Sandbox) under your Organization's root, and move or invite a second account into it if you have one available. Write a real SCP JSON document denying one specific service action, and explain in writing why attaching it to the OU would restrict even that account's own root user.
slots.deliverable: A real Organizational Unit created under your Organization, plus a written SCP JSON document and a written explanation of why an SCP overrides even root-level permissions in every account under it.

lessons.title: Launching and Sizing an EC2 Instance

slots.practicalActivity: Run a real aws ec2 run-instances command specifying --image-id, --instance-type t3.micro, --subnet-id, and a block-device-mapping for a 20GB gp3 root volume, once deliberately omitting --key-name and --security-group-ids to see what you get, then relaunch correctly with both included. Use aws ec2 describe-instances to confirm the final instance's real subnet, type, and root volume size match what you requested.
slots.deliverable: Real run-instances output for two launches (one missing key-name/security-group-ids, one complete) plus describe-instances output confirming the final instance's actual subnet, instance type, and 20GB gp3 root volume.

lessons.title: Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) and the EC2 Lifecycle

slots.practicalActivity: Install one piece of software on a running EC2 instance, run aws ec2 create-image --no-reboot to capture it as a custom AMI, and launch a second instance from that AMI confirming the software is already present. Separately, stop one instance and terminate another, then compare their states with describe-instances and check the EBS console to see the different outcomes for each instance's root volume.
slots.deliverable: A real custom AMI built from a modified instance, a second instance launched from it with the software already present, plus describe-instances and EBS console evidence of stop vs. terminate behaving differently on the root volume.

lessons.title: EC2 Instance Types and Choosing the Right Family

slots.practicalActivity: Run aws ec2 describe-instance-types filtered to each of the four families (t, m, c, r) and record the real vCPU and memory numbers for one size in each. For 3 real workload scenarios of your own choosing, write one sentence each naming the family you'd pick, citing the actual vCPU/memory numbers you just pulled.
slots.deliverable: Real describe-instance-types output recording vCPU and memory for one size in each of the T/M/C/R families, plus 3 written workload-to-family recommendations citing those real numbers.

lessons.title: Key Pairs, Security Groups, and Connecting to an Instance

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real key pair with aws ec2 create-key-pair, save the private key and chmod 400 it, create a security group that denies all inbound by default, then add exactly one inbound rule allowing SSH only from your own current public IP (found with curl checkip.amazonaws.com) instead of 0.0.0.0/0. Launch an instance with both and connect with ssh -i pointing at your real private key file.
slots.deliverable: A real key pair file with correct file permissions, a security group scoped to your own IP on port 22 only, and a successful ssh -i connection into a real running instance.

lessons.title: S3 Buckets, Objects, and Storage Classes

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real S3 bucket with a globally-unique name using aws s3api create-bucket, upload one file to it at S3 Standard with aws s3 cp, upload the same file again under a different key with --storage-class GLACIER, then run aws s3api list-objects-v2 to see both objects' real StorageClass values in the output.
slots.deliverable: A real S3 bucket containing the same file uploaded twice under different keys at two different storage classes, confirmed with list-objects-v2 output showing each object's actual StorageClass field.

lessons.title: S3 Versioning, Lifecycle Rules, and Access Control

slots.practicalActivity: Enable versioning on your bucket from last session, overwrite the same object key twice more, then run aws s3api list-object-versions to see all 3 versions. Delete the object with a plain aws s3 rm and confirm with list-object-versions that a delete marker was added rather than the data disappearing, then write and apply a real lifecycle.json rule transitioning a prefix to GLACIER after 30 days, and run put-public-access-block with all four flags set to true.
slots.deliverable: list-object-versions output showing 3 real versions plus a delete marker after deletion, an applied lifecycle rule confirmed with get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration, and Block Public Access confirmed enabled on the bucket.

lessons.title: EBS Volumes and How They Attach to EC2

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real 10GB gp3 EBS volume in the same Availability Zone as a running instance, attach it with aws ec2 attach-volume, SSH in and format/mount it, write a test file to it, then detach it and attempt to attach it to an instance you've confirmed is in a different Availability Zone, capturing the resulting error.
slots.deliverable: A real gp3 volume created, attached, formatted, and mounted with a test file written to it, plus the real error message proving the same volume can't attach to an instance in a different AZ.

lessons.title: EBS Snapshots and Backup Strategy

slots.practicalActivity: Take a real snapshot of last session's volume with aws ec2 create-snapshot, create a brand-new volume from that snapshot in a different Availability Zone, attach it to an instance there, and confirm your test file from the prior lesson is present. Then write out a real Data Lifecycle Manager policy targeting a tag like Backup=daily with a 7-day retention.
slots.deliverable: A real snapshot restored into a new volume in a different AZ with your original test file intact, plus a written DLM policy specifying the exact tag it targets and its retention period.

lessons.title: VPC Fundamentals and CIDR Planning

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real VPC with a 10.60.0.0/16 CIDR block, carve out two /24 subnets in two different Availability Zones, then deliberately attempt a third subnet with an overlapping CIDR range and capture AWS rejecting it. For one subnet, calculate and write out by hand the 5 addresses AWS reserves and how many usable addresses remain.
slots.deliverable: A real VPC with two non-overlapping subnets in two AZs, the captured error from the rejected overlapping-CIDR attempt, and a hand-worked calculation of one subnet's 5 reserved addresses and usable count.

lessons.title: Public vs. Private Subnets and Internet Gateways

slots.practicalActivity: Create and attach a real Internet Gateway to your VPC from last session, point one subnet's route table at it, and run modify-subnet-attribute --map-public-ip-on-launch on that subnet only. Launch one instance into that subnet and one into the still-private subnet, then compare their public IPs in describe-instances to confirm only the first one received one.
slots.deliverable: A real attached Internet Gateway, one subnet correctly configured as public (route plus map-public-ip-on-launch) and one left private, with describe-instances output proving only the public-subnet instance got a public IP.

lessons.title: Route Tables, NAT Gateways, and Outbound Internet Access

slots.practicalActivity: Allocate a real Elastic IP, create a NAT Gateway in your public subnet with it, and point your private subnet's route table at the NAT Gateway instead of leaving it with no internet route. SSH into the private-subnet instance via the public instance as a bastion and confirm it can now reach the internet outbound (e.g. a package update) while still having no direct inbound path from your own machine.
slots.deliverable: A real NAT Gateway with an Elastic IP, a private subnet's route table pointed at it, and proof that the private instance reaches the internet outbound while remaining unreachable directly from outside the VPC.

lessons.title: Security Groups vs. Network ACLs in AWS

slots.practicalActivity: Create a custom Network ACL (starting deny-all), associate it with your public subnet, add a numbered rule allowing inbound HTTPS and a second rule allowing outbound traffic on the ephemeral port range 1024-65535, then deliberately remove the ephemeral-port outbound rule and confirm from outside that HTTPS responses stop coming back even though the Security Group never changed. Restore the rule and confirm it works again.
slots.deliverable: A real custom NACL on your public subnet with numbered inbound/outbound rules, plus before/after proof that removing the ephemeral-port outbound rule alone breaks return traffic despite an unchanged Security Group.

lessons.title: Configuring and Using the AWS CLI

slots.practicalActivity: Run aws configure for your default profile, then run aws configure --profile lab to create a second named profile. Open both ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config in a text editor and write a note pointing out exactly where the "profile" prefix appears for the named profile versus the default.
slots.deliverable: Two real configured profiles across ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.aws/config, plus a written note showing the exact section-naming difference you found between the two files.

lessons.title: Managing Resources with AWS CLI Commands

slots.practicalActivity: Run aws ec2 describe-instances, aws s3 ls, and aws iam list-users with no flags, then rerun the EC2 command three times with --output table, --output json, and --output text to compare the same data. Build your own --query JMESPath expression (not copied from the lesson) that flattens Reservations[].Instances[] and pulls InstanceId, InstanceType, and State.Name into a table.
slots.deliverable: Real output from the same describe-instances call in all 3 output formats, plus a working custom --query expression producing a clean table of your real instances.

lessons.title: AWS CloudShell and Scripting Basics

slots.practicalActivity: Open AWS CloudShell from the console, confirm you're already authenticated by running aws sts get-caller-identity with no prior setup, then write and run a script that loops over every real bucket in your account printing its object count and total size (modeled on the lesson's example). Save it to CloudShell's persistent storage, close the session, reopen CloudShell, and confirm the script is still there.
slots.deliverable: A real script run successfully in CloudShell looping over your actual S3 buckets, plus confirmation that the saved script persisted after closing and reopening the session.

lessons.title: Tagging Resources for Organization and Cost Tracking

slots.practicalActivity: Tag 2-3 existing EC2 instances with aws ec2 create-tags using Environment and Team keys, then launch one new instance with the same tags applied at launch via --tag-specifications. Run describe-instances filtered by --filters "Name=tag:Environment,Value=..." to confirm only the tagged instances return, then activate your Environment tag as a user-defined Cost Allocation Tag in Billing.
slots.deliverable: Real instances tagged both after the fact and at launch time, a filtered describe-instances query proving the tag filter works, and your Environment tag shown as activated in the Cost Allocation Tags console.

lessons.title: CloudWatch Metrics and Dashboards

slots.practicalActivity: In the CloudWatch console, find the automatic CPUUtilization, NetworkIn/Out, and StatusCheckFailed metrics already being recorded for a real EC2 instance with no setup. Publish a real custom metric with aws cloudwatch put-metric-data under your own namespace, then build a CloudWatch Dashboard with at least 2 widgets showing your custom metric and that instance's real CPUUtilization side by side.
slots.deliverable: A real CloudWatch Dashboard with at least 2 widgets, one showing a genuinely published custom metric and the other showing an instance's real, automatically-collected CPUUtilization.

lessons.title: CloudWatch Alarms and Notifications

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real SNS topic, subscribe your own email, and click the confirmation link AWS sends you. Create a real CloudWatch alarm on one instance's CPUUtilization (threshold 80%, one 300-second evaluation period) pointed at your topic, then actually trigger it by running a CPU-stress command on the instance until it transitions to ALARM and you receive the real notification email.
slots.deliverable: A real SNS topic with a confirmed email subscription, a CloudWatch alarm that genuinely transitioned from OK to ALARM under real CPU load, and the received notification email as proof.

lessons.title: CloudWatch Logs and Log Groups

slots.practicalActivity: Install and configure the real CloudWatch Agent on an EC2 instance with a JSON config shipping one real log file (e.g. /var/log/syslog) to a new log group, confirm log events arriving in the CloudWatch Logs console, then run a real CloudWatch Logs Insights query filtering for a specific keyword and sorting by @timestamp descending.
slots.deliverable: A real log group receiving live log events from the CloudWatch Agent on your instance, plus a working Logs Insights query and its actual result rows.

lessons.title: CloudTrail and Tracking Who Did What

slots.practicalActivity: Open CloudTrail's Event History and find a real RunInstances or StopInstances event from one of your own earlier labs, noting its actual IAM identity ARN, timestamp, and source IP. Create a real multi-region Trail delivering to a new S3 bucket, then run aws cloudtrail lookup-events filtering on EventName=StopInstances to pull the same kind of evidence from the CLI.
slots.deliverable: A real CloudTrail Event History entry from your own account activity with its ARN/timestamp/IP recorded, plus a working multi-region Trail delivering to S3 and matching lookup-events output for the same event type.

lessons.title: Understanding the AWS Bill and Cost Explorer

slots.practicalActivity: Open Billing and Cost Management and record your account's actual current-period total. In Cost Explorer, group the last 3 months of spend by Service to see what's really costing money, then switch the grouping to Tag (using a real tag from an earlier lesson if you have one) to see spend broken out by what you've tagged. Write one sentence on what the forecast is currently projecting.
slots.deliverable: Real Cost Explorer screenshots grouped by Service and then by Tag for your own account's actual spend, plus a written sentence stating the current forecast and what it is and isn't accounting for.

lessons.title: AWS Budgets and Cost Alerts

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real AWS Budget scoped to your account with a modest monthly amount sized to your real usage, set one alert threshold at 80% on actual spend and a second at 100% on forecasted spend, and subscribe your own email to both. Confirm in the Budgets console that it's actively tracking real spend against the limit.
slots.deliverable: A real AWS Budget with two alert thresholds (80% actual, 100% forecasted) both subscribed to your email, confirmed actively tracking your account's real spend in the console.

lessons.title: Right-Sizing and Common Cost Optimization Levers

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real EC2 instance and pull its CPUUtilization history from CloudWatch to judge whether it's oversized for what it's actually doing. Separately, run aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available to find any real unattached EBS volumes left over from earlier labs, and delete the ones you don't need.
slots.deliverable: A real CPUUtilization-based right-sizing judgment for one instance citing the actual metric data, plus describe-volumes output showing unattached volumes found and deleted.

lessons.title: Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, and Spot Instances

slots.practicalActivity: In the console, open the Savings Plans and Reserved Instances recommendation pages (no purchase required) and record what AWS actually recommends for your account's real usage, even if it recommends nothing yet. Then submit one real Spot Instance request with aws ec2 request-spot-instances for a throwaway t3.micro and compare its actual spot price to that type's On-Demand rate.
slots.deliverable: Real screenshots of your account's actual RI/Savings Plan recommendations, plus a real Spot Instance request with its actual spot price recorded next to the equivalent On-Demand rate.

lessons.title: Lab: Deploying a Small Multi-Tier Environment in AWS
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Deploying and Administering an AWS Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Build the Meridian Outfitters environment from the lesson for real: a VPC with a public and a private subnet, an Internet Gateway attached and routed to the public subnet with map-public-ip-on-launch enabled, two security groups (still unscoped), a web instance launched into the public subnet with a public IP, an app instance launched into the private subnet with none, and a real S3 bucket for shared app data.
slots.deliverable: A real multi-tier environment matching Meridian's shape — one VPC, a public and private subnet, an attached and routed Internet Gateway, two EC2 instances with correctly different public-IP outcomes, and a real S3 bucket for app data.

lessons.title: Lab: Securing and Monitoring the Environment
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Deploying and Administering an AWS Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Scope your web security group to allow only 443/80 from 0.0.0.0/0 and 22 from your own real IP; scope the app security group to allow port 8080 only --source-group pointing at the web security group; create a real IAM role with S3 access attached to the app instance as an instance profile instead of any access key; set a real CloudWatch alarm on the web instance's CPUUtilization notifying an SNS topic; take an EBS snapshot of the app instance's root volume; and create an AWS Budget capped to a real dollar amount for this lab environment.
slots.deliverable: Both security groups correctly scoped (one by CIDR, one by --source-group), a real IAM role/instance profile on the app instance with zero hardcoded keys, a working CloudWatch alarm, a real EBS snapshot, and an active AWS Budget, all built against your own Lesson 29 environment.

lessons.title: Case Study: Troubleshooting an Unreachable Instance
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Deploying and Administering an AWS Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately recreate Meridian's mistake in your own lab: launch a new instance into your private subnet by accident (reusing the wrong --subnet-id on purpose), then run the lesson's exact four-command diagnostic sequence yourself — instance state, public IP, subnet ID, then the subnet's route table — to find the real root cause before fixing it by terminating and relaunching into the correct public subnet.
slots.deliverable: Real CLI output from all four diagnostic commands run against your own deliberately-misplaced instance, correctly identifying the wrong-subnet root cause, plus proof of the instance successfully relaunched with a public IP in the correct subnet.

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: AWS Administration Review
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Deploying and Administering an AWS Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Run a closing verification pass against your own Lesson 29-31 environment: confirm the IAM role (not a key) is still attached to the app instance, confirm both security groups are still correctly scoped, confirm the CloudWatch alarm and AWS Budget are both still active, and use CloudTrail's lookup-events to find the real instance call from your Lesson 31 fix, noting its actual IAM identity ARN. Write your own one-paragraph resume bullet describing this capstone build using the specific AWS services you actually used.
slots.deliverable: A written end-to-end verification of your own environment covering identity, networking, monitoring, and cost controls, a real CloudTrail lookup-events result identifying who performed your Lesson 31 fix, and a written resume bullet naming the specific AWS services used.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can administer a real multi-tier AWS environment end to end — retiring the root account in favor of IAM users, groups, roles, and instance profiles; launching, sizing, and imaging EC2 instances; choosing between S3 storage classes and EBS volume types and protecting both with versioning, lifecycle rules, and snapshots; designing a VPC with public and private subnets, Internet and NAT gateways, and the right mix of security groups and NACLs; scripting against AWS from the CLI and CloudShell; monitoring with CloudWatch metrics, alarms, logs, and CloudTrail; and managing real AWS spend with Cost Explorer, Budgets, and right-sizing — and has personally deployed, secured, monitored, and debugged one real multi-tier environment from a live incident through to a full administrative review.
